blocked.name: Braise
blocking: The `start` facet never forks the tree, so the browned/raw decision — the standfirst's second promise and the entire subject of the 'On the first fork' note — is drawn exactly once on the whole page. Cause: the trie in src/lib/canon.ts flattens all chips of an earlier facet before reaching the next one, so a dish-unique chip anywhere in facet[0] ends that branch. Every one of the sixteen finish cells carries a dish-unique second chip ('glossy from the flour', 'clings to the meat', 'strained into gravy', …), so in the 'By what you end up with' nesting [finish > start > liquid] the trie collapses each dish into a singleton at depth 2 and start never forks at all; the only place browned-vs-raw appears anywhere is under 'water · enough to cover' in the 'By liquid' tree, separating Gulyás from Ghormeh sabzi. Fix as rice did: keep `finish` to the three-value decision and move the dish-unique refinement out of the nested path. Concretely — add a sixth facet {"id":"body","label":"What thickens it"} that appears in no `by` list (CanonViews renders every facet as a column, so nothing is lost from the table), move each finish cell's trailing chips into it, and leave finish as ["reduces to a sauce"] / ["stays a broth"] / ["the liquid cooks away"]. I ran this through the real builder: it produces 'reduces to a sauce > meat browned first > {Boeuf bourguignon, Pot roast, Ghormeh sabzi, Korma, Seco de cordero}' and 'reduces to a sauce > meat goes in raw > {Pörkölt, Tagine, Doro wat, Massaman, Adobo+Humba, Kare-kare}', which is the fork the family is about. Note that the 'What thickens it' note ends 'Look down the finish column' — after this change it should say the thickening column, which is also more accurate, since doro wat's onions are not in the finish column today.

The 'On the first fork' note is false for six of the ten dishes it describes. It claims the ten non-browning rows 'put raw meat into an aromatic base that has already been cooked'. Only four do: Gulyás and Pörkölt ('onions fried first'), Doro wat ('onions cooked dry without fat') and Massaman ('paste fried in cracked coconut cream'). The other six contradict it in their own chips — Tagine 'turned in the spices cold', Rendang 'into the spice paste cold', Adobo and Humba 'marinated in the braising liquid', Birria 'marinated in the chilli paste', and Kare-kare 'oxtail simmered plain for hours', which starts with no aromatics in the pot at all. Worse, the note offers 'a pounded paste for rendang' as one of its three examples, and rendang's own start chip says the paste goes in cold. Rewrite the note around what the table actually shows: six sear, and the other ten skip the sear for two different reasons — a base cooked first (gulyás, pörkölt, doro wat, massaman), or a raw paste or marinade that would scorch if it were hot enough to brown meat (tagine, rendang, adobo, humba, birria) — with kare-kare a third case that starts in plain water and adds everything later.

The korma note's 'The only liquid here that splits if it boils' is contradicted by the rendang note four rows down, which is built on coconut milk splitting: 'Once the coconut milk breaks the pot is frying.' Coconut milk splits, and so does the cream korma's own cell lists as its second liquid. Change the claim to the one that is true and sharper — korma is the only dish here where splitting ruins it, whereas rendang is cooked until the milk breaks on purpose. Something like: 'The only liquid here that must not split. Rendang's breaks on purpose; yoghurt's is the end of the dish, which is why low heat in a korma is not patience but the entire constraint.'

Humba is drawn as a root node in the 'By region' tree, cut off from the parent the file itself declares. Because its region cell is the single chip ["Visayas"] while Adobo and Kare-kare carry ["Philippines"], the shipped tree renders '• Visayas — vinegar — Humba' as a sibling of 'Philippines', 'China' and 'Peru' — so the one true descent in the family is invisible in the reading where it would be most legible, and the Visayas is drawn as a peer of the Philippines rather than part of it. Four other cells have the same mixed-granularity problem (Burgundy, Jalisco, West Sumatra, Mughal India are sub-national roots sitting among nations). Use the two-chip broad-then-specific form that noodle-soup.json already uses (["Japan","Tokyo"], ["Vietnam","Huế"]): Humba ["Philippines","Visayas"], Boeuf bourguignon ["France","Burgundy"], Birria ["Mexico","Jalisco"], Rendang ["Indonesia","West Sumatra"], and give Korma a modern country plus the historical qualifier rather than ["Mughal India"] alone. Verified with the real builder: this draws 'Philippines > {vinegar — Adobo, Visayas — vinegar — Humba, water — Kare-kare}', putting Humba inside the Philippines beside its parent, and the single-dish countries collapse harmlessly to one line ('France — Burgundy — wine — Boeuf bourguignon').

The `root` line 'Tough meat · a little liquid · low heat · hours' is contradicted by the table it defines. 'A little liquid' is wrong for three rows: Gulyás and Ghormeh sabzi both read 'enough to cover', and Kare-kare's oxtail is simmered for hours in water 'which becomes the stock' — and the family deliberately includes two dishes that stay broths, which the standfirst is honest about ('whether that liquid ends up a sauce or stays a broth') while the root line is not. 'Tough meat' is also wrong for Hong shao rou, which is pork belly — fatty and collagen-rich, but grilled all over Asia. (Doro wat's chicken is defensible if it is a mature bird, so I would leave that alone.) Rewrite the root as something the sixteen rows all satisfy, e.g. 'A cut that needs time · liquid in a covered pot · low heat · hours', and if you keep the standfirst's 'a cut too tough to grill', make it 'a cut that will not cook fast' so the belly and the hen both fit.
reasons: File reviewed: /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/data/canon/braise.json (16 dishes, 5 facets, 3 nestings + descent). I rebuilt the trie from /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/src/lib/canon.ts in a scratch script and rendered all four readings, so every structural claim below is about what the page actually draws, not about the JSON in the abstract. I also checked the region convention against the other fourteen families in data/canon/ and confirmed in src/components/canon/CanonViews.tsx that every facet renders as a table column whether or not a nesting uses it.

Check 1 (uniqueness) — clean. No two rows match. The closest pair is Adobo/Humba, which share every chip on the 'By liquid' path and are drawn as two leaves under one branch ('vinegar · soy sauce · meat goes in raw · marinated in the braising liquid · reduces to a sauce'); they separate on the last finish chip, two base chips and region, and Humba earns its row. Gulyás/Pörkölt differ in exactly two chips — liquid[1] ('enough to cover' vs 'barely any') and the whole finish cell — which is the point the pörkölt note makes, so that is a feature.

Check 2 (dead dimensions) — no column is literally constant: liquid has 12 distinct lead chips, finish 3, start 2, region 15 across 16 rows. But `start` is functionally dead in the drawn trees — it forks the page exactly once. See blocking item 1. `base` is in no nesting, which is house-normal (dough-with-filling leaves `filling` unnested) and it still renders as a column, so that is fine.

Check 3 (compound chips) — clean. No chip contains a comma or an 'and'. Kare-kare correctly splits its two thickeners into 'ground peanuts stirred in' and 'toasted rice stirred in' rather than joining them, which is the exact mistake this check exists to catch.

Check 4 (multi-chip ordering) — the ordering itself is right everywhere: liquid leads with the substance ('water' 6x, 'coconut milk' 2x, 'vinegar' 2x) then the quantity or the second liquid; start leads with 'meat browned first'/'meat goes in raw' in all sixteen rows; finish leads with one of three buckets in all sixteen. The defect is not the order within the cell but that the chip immediately after the shared lead is dish-unique in every finish cell, which terminates the branch before the next facet is reached. See blocking item 1.

Check 5 (parent) — correct. Humba → Adobo is the one real descent here and it is marked; the 'By descent' reading draws fifteen roots with Humba under Adobo. Gulyás and Pörkölt are rightly left as siblings rather than parent/child, since neither descends from the other. Massaman/Rendang and Adobo/Hong shao rou are similarities, not lineage, and correctly carry no parent.

Check 6 (coverage) — not parochial. Thirteen countries across five continents, three European rows out of sixteen, and the non-European entries are specific dishes rather than one representative each: two Hungarian, three Philippine, two Southeast Asian coconut-milk rows taken to opposite ends. Good.

Check 7 (names and facts) — mostly right. Verified: gulyás is the soup and pörkölt is what the world calls goulash; paprika off the heat; the tagine cone condensing and returning steam; doro wat's dry onions before any fat; rendang's coconut milk breaking into a fry; massaman's paste in cracked coconut cream; adobo's vinegar as preservation; tausi and dried banana blossom in humba; kare-kare's toasted rice and bagoong at the table; hong shao rou's caramel before anything else; birria's consomé; seco meaning thick rather than dry, with beer standing in for chicha. Two claims are wrong (blocking items 2 and 3) and two are soft: the humba note calls hong shao rou its 'other ancestor' when the usual derivation is from Hokkien hong ba/hong bak, a relative of red-braising rather than that dish specifically; and ghormeh sabzi's base omits leek or chives (tareh), which is one of the defining herbs alongside the parsley and fenugreek.

Check 8 (standfirst) — the standfirst is the strongest part of the file. It says what the method is, names the four decisions the columns actually hold, and does not praise the food. The `root` line beneath it does not clear the same bar (blocking item 5).

Non-blocking, worth a pass if you are in the file anyway. (a) `yours` will miss five of the sixteen dishes: no fragment matches doro wat, ghormeh sabzi, hong shao rou, humba or seco, and a recipe titled 'Gulyás' will not match 'goulash' — add 'wat', 'ghormeh', 'hong shao', 'humba', 'seco', 'gulyas'. (b) Two chips are descriptions rather than decisions: tagine's 'the conical lid returns the steam' is a fact about the pot, and kare-kare's 'which becomes the stock' is an outcome; both read oddly as siblings of 'barely any' and 'beef stock'. (c) The 'What thickens it' note says pörkölt uses 'nothing at all except leaving the lid off', but its fried onions do the same job doro wat's collapsed onions are credited with two clauses earlier; and pot roast's 'strained into gravy' makes it a borrower too, which the note's list omits. (d) Adobo's finish chip 'the meat fried in the last of it' sits under 'reduces to a sauce' while note 2 says only rendang and hong shao rou go past sauce — adopting blocking item 1 removes the chip from the tree, so decide whether that step is real before moving it.

blocked.name: Fermented vegetables
blocking: /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/data/canon/fermented-vegetable.json — the root and standfirst are falsified by their own table three times over. (a) 'kept from the air' / 'packed away from the air': Nukazuke's own chip is 'turned by hand every day' — the bran bed is deliberately aerated daily, that is how it is controlled — and Gari's is 'pressed in a sack', which is porous by design. (b) 'raw vegetable': Curtido is 'cabbage scalded first', Gajar gobhi is 'blanched and sun-dried first', Zha cai is 'air-dried first'. (c) 'the bacteria already on its skin': four rows carry an explicit 'a starter' chip — Pao cai's mother brine, Nukazuke's decades-old bran bed, Dua cai chua's rice water, Salgam suyu's bulgur sourdough — which is the fork the `add` column exists to draw. Rewrite both so the table cannot contradict them: root to something like 'Raw or barely scalded vegetable · held under brine or packed tight · lactic bacteria, wild or fed from a living bed'; standfirst opening to 'Every one of these is a vegetable held under salt or its own juice until lactic bacteria turn it sour — the ones that came in on it, or the ones living in a bed the cook keeps going.' The second half of the standfirst is the good half and should stand.

/Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/data/canon/fermented-vegetable.json — Kimchi's `salt` cell leads with 'salted and rinsed first', a chip no other dish shares, so in the primary nesting Kimchi is not under 'dry-salted' or 'submerged in brine' at all: it renders as a fourth top-level branch of its own, floating beside the three routes the 'On salt' note says exist ('Brining and dry-salting are two routes to the same brine'). Its own note also says which route it takes — 'brined to draw water out, rinsed so it is not inedible'. Make the cell lead with the route and keep the double-salting as the chips after it: ["submerged in brine", "rinsed after salting", "drained overnight"]. I verified this drops Kimchi under the brine branch without disturbing anything else. (If you would rather call baechu salting dry — both methods are real — then lead with 'dry-salted' and fix the note to match; what cannot stand is a leading chip that is neither.)

/Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/data/canon/fermented-vegetable.json — the primary nesting 'By how the salt goes in' ['salt','add','keep'] renders identically to ['salt'] alone. Every dish's second salt chip is unique, so nothing forks below level one: the tree is three branches (plus Kimchi's orphan) over sixteen flat leaves whose labels are collapsed chains of up to seven chips — the Zha cai leaf currently reads 'salted and pressed three times — air-dried first — chilli paste — sichuan peppercorn — room temperature — sealed in earthenware — Zha cai'. The cause is vocabulary drift: three dishes describe the same move in three words ('pressed under a weight' / 'pressed under a stone' / 'weighted under the surface'), and four describe pre-wilting in four ('air-dried first' / 'wilted in the sun first' / 'blanched and sun-dried first' / 'cabbage scalded first'). Two of those are also compound chips — 'salted and pressed three times' and 'blanched and sun-dried first' are each two moves in one chip, which is check 3. Normalise the second chip and put the dish-specific detail third. I tested this exact set: Suan cai ["dry-salted","pressed under a weight","topped up with water"]; Ogorki ["submerged in brine","pressed under a weight"]; Zha cai ["dry-salted","wilted first","pressed three times"]; Gajar gobhi ["dry-salted","wilted first","blanched"]; Dua cai chua ["submerged in brine","wilted first"]; Curtido ["dry-salted","scalded first"]. It produces 'dry-salted > pressed under a weight > {Sauerkraut, Suan cai}' and 'dry-salted > wilted first > {Zha cai, Gajar gobhi shalgam achar}' — two forks that are exactly what the family is about, where today there are none.

/Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/data/canon/fermented-vegetable.json — the 'On where you stop' note ends 'Everything in the crunchy column is cold, or fast, or both.' Zha cai's own row says room temperature, sealed in earthenware, three to six months, stays crunchy: neither cold nor fast, and the most famously crunchy thing in the table. Torshi left (room temperature, two weeks) strains the claim too. The exception is already explained one screen up in Zha cai's own note, so use it: '...is cold, or fast, or both — except zha cai, which is pressed so dry three times over that there is little water left in it to soften.' As written, a reader who has just read the zha cai row catches the note out.

/Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/data/canon/fermented-vegetable.json — three region cells are two places joined into one chip with the display separator: "Germany · Alsace", "Fuling · Chongqing", "Iraq · Levant". The trie forks on chips, so a joined chip can never fork, and the column also mixes scales (city 'Adana', province 'Sichuan', region 'Punjab', country 'Japan', continent-slice 'West Africa'). The result is that 'By region' draws 14 of 16 dishes as top-level leaves — only Korea and Punjab fork — and the three Chinese pickles, one of the most interesting groupings available (dry-salt in the northeast, brine in Sichuan, press in Chongqing), never meet. Split the joined chips and lead with the broadest shared unit: Sauerkraut ["Germany","Alsace"], Suan cai ["China","Northeast"], Pao cai ["China","Sichuan"], Zha cai ["China","Chongqing","Fuling"], Torshi left ["Iraq","Levant"], Salgam suyu ["Turkey","Adana"], Kanji and Gajar gobhi both ["India","Punjab"]. I rendered it: China gathers three, Korea keeps its two, 'India · Punjab' gathers two, and the reading finally does something.

/Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/data/canon/fermented-vegetable.json — Kimchi's `add` cell reads ["chilli paste","gochugaru","garlic","salted shrimp"]. Gochujang — the thing 'chilli paste' names in this table, since Zha cai carries the identical chip for the real chilli paste it is rubbed with — is not an ingredient of baechu kimchi; the yangnyeom is built from gochugaru powder, which the very next chip already says. So the chip is both redundant and wrong, and because it is an exact string match it would falsely fork Kimchi and Zha cai together on any reading that leads with `add` (I confirmed this in the ['add','salt'] probe: 'chilli paste > {Kimchi, Zha cai}'). Replace with 'a seasoning paste' or simply drop it: ["gochugaru","garlic","ginger","salted shrimp"].

/Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/data/canon/fermented-vegetable.json — the Salgam suyu note claims 'The turnip and black carrot are strained out and the brine is served cold beside kebab. The one entry here where the pickle is thrown away.' The family's own cited source (Wikipedia, Turnip water) says the opposite on both counts: a slice of purple carrot, and often garlic or pepper, is added to the glass just before drinking, and the drink is built on the brine of black-carrot pickles with the aromatic turnip fermented in alongside — the carrot is the substrate, not the flavouring. So the `end` chip 'the vegetable is only the flavouring' and the 'thrown away' line both need to go, and with them the contrast the file draws against Kanji's 'the carrot is eaten after', which is not a real difference. Suggested: `end` ["you drink the liquid","the turnip is the aromatic, the carrot the ferment"], and a note that says the black carrot does the fermenting, the turnip flavours it, and a slice of the carrot goes back into the glass.

/Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/data/canon/fermented-vegetable.json — the Kanji note says the Adana answer was reached 'with mustard doing the work of the bulgur'. The bulgur sourdough is an inoculum, which is why Salgam suyu carries the chip 'a starter'; ground mustard is not, which is why Kanji correctly does not. Mustard seed contributes pungency and antimicrobial isothiocyanates that keep the wrong organisms down while the carrots' own lactobacilli work — the opposite job. The table is right and the sentence is wrong. Rewrite along the lines of: '...the same answer Adana arrived at, except that nothing is added to start it — the mustard keeps the competition down and the carrots bring their own bacteria.'

/Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/data/canon/fermented-vegetable.json — the 'On salt' note ends 'Gundruk and gari dismiss the doorman entirely and rely on speed and an airtight pot instead.' True of gundruk (its chip is 'sealed in an earthen pot'); false of gari, whose chip is 'pressed in a sack' — a porous sack under weight, where the protection is the pressing-out of liquid and the sheer speed, not a seal. Fix to something both rows satisfy: '...rely on speed instead, and on shutting the air out by sealing the pot or pressing the mash dry.'
reasons: File reviewed: /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/data/canon/fermented-vegetable.json (16 dishes, 5 facets, 3 nestings). I reimplemented grow()/collapse() from /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/src/lib/canon.ts in a scratch script and rendered all three authored nestings, plus four variants, so every structural claim below is about what the page will actually draw.

Check 1 (uniqueness) passes. No two rows are identical and no pair differs in only one cell. The closest pair is Torshi left / Salgam suyu, which share an identical `salt` cell (["submerged in brine"]) and an identical `keep` cell (["room temperature","two weeks"]) but part company on `add`, `end` and `region` — two different dishes, correctly.

Check 2 (dead dimensions): nothing is constant — salt has 14 distinct cells / 4 leading chips, add 14/7, keep 14/5, end 16/4, region 14/14. But `add` never occupies a leading slot in any of the three nestings, and it is the best-forking column in the file. I ran ['add','salt'] as a probe: it draws 'a starter > {Pao cai, Nukazuke, Dua cai chua, Salgam suyu}', 'nothing at all · no salt at all > {Gundruk, Gari}', 'nothing but salt · dry-salted > {Sauerkraut, Suan cai}', 'garlic > {Ogorki, Dongchimi, Torshi left}', 'ground mustard seed > {Kanji, Gajar gobhi}'. That is the living-culture-versus-wild argument the 'On salt' note gestures at, and it is currently unreadable. Recommend a fourth nesting {"label": "By what goes in with it", "by": ["add","salt"]}.

Same problem, worse, for `keep`: the standfirst names temperature and time as two of its four decisions and the 'On where you stop' note turns entirely on them, but `keep` sits third in one nesting where every path is already unique, so the reader can never sort the family by it. Its vocabulary is clean and would fork immediately — I rendered {"label": "By how it is kept", "by": ["keep","salt","end"]} and it gives five top-level branches (cool cellar 2, cold from the start 2, room temperature 7, warm kitchen 3, in the sun 2) with real second-level forks ('room temperature > two weeks · submerged in brine > {Torshi left, Salgam suyu}', 'warm kitchen > two to three days > {Dua cai chua, Curtido}'). This is the strongest reading the data can support and it is not offered.

Check 4: `end` leads consistently with the texture/form chip, which is why 'By what it becomes' is the best of the three authored readings — it forks 5 / 7 / 2 / 2 at the top and again at 'stays crunchy > barely sour > {Pao cai, Nukazuke}', a genuinely surprising pairing. `salt` leads consistently too, except Kimchi (blocking 2). `add` and `keep` lead correctly but are never reached.

Check 5 (parent) is correctly absent, and the 'On depth' note defends it accurately: kimchi is not dongchimi plus paste, sauerkraut and suan cai are convergent, kanji and salgam are convergent. Worth knowing for the author: since commit 34b764f, nestingsFor() adds 'By descent' alongside the facet nestings instead of replacing them, so a `parent` link no longer costs a family its other readings — but none is warranted here.

Check 6 (coverage) passes and is one of the file's real strengths: Germany/Alsace, Poland, three Chinese regions, Korea x2, Japan, Vietnam, Iraq/Levant, Adana, Punjab x2, El Salvador, Nepal, West Africa. Asia carries 10 of 16, which is defensible for this technique. The salt-brine-versus-vinegar line is scoped honestly in the Torshi note. Optional gap: the Balkan/Slavic whole-head sour cabbage (turshija / kiseli kupus, brined whole, cold, months) is the one large tradition missing, and it would be a genuine third answer beside sauerkraut's dry salt and suan cai's stone.

Check 7: most of it holds up against the cited sources. Gundruk verified salt-free, earthen pot, about a week warm, then sun-dried (Wikipedia, listed in sources). Zha cai as the swollen stem of Brassica juncea var. tumida from Fuling, air-dried, pressed repeatedly, rubbed with chilli and Sichuan pepper — correct, and Fuling is indeed in Chongqing. Pao cai's water-sealed jar, mother brine and no-oil rule — correct. Dongchimi predating chilli in Korea — correct. Kanji's four-to-six days in the sun matches the three-to-seven days the sources give. Gari's ferment as cyanogen removal, ended by toasting — correct. Five claims do not hold and are in blocking.

Check 8: the standfirst is specific rather than admiring and names all four decisions the facets carry, which is what the check asks. But its central premise is falsified by its own table in three separate ways — see blocking 1.

Non-blocking coherence flag: Ogorki kiszone is the one dish whose note claims an ingredient exists purely to protect texture ('the one ingredient here whose job is texture'), and it is filed under 'goes soft' while Curtido, which adds nothing of the kind, is filed under 'stays crunchy'. Not a contradiction — the leaf slows softening rather than preventing it — but a reader comparing the two rows will stumble. Either change the `end` chip to something like 'softens slowly' or have the note say the leaf buys weeks rather than crunch.

Non-blocking: 'On depth' says kimchi and dongchimi 'both descend from the same salted radish'. Early kimchi as salted radish and other vegetables is fair, but modern baechu kimchi is built on napa cabbage, which only reached Korea in the nineteenth century. 'Both descend from the same habit of salting vegetables down for winter' would survive a reader who looks it up, and costs nothing.

Non-blocking: Curtido's honesty about the scald ('The scald is argued over') is the right register for a contested step, and Gari's inclusion — a starch staple in a vegetable family — is earned by the root rather than smuggled. Both are good calls.

blocked.name: Fried chicken
blocking: Southern fried chicken and Broasted chicken have `after: []`, and the empty cell breaks two readings. In 'By what happens after' the builder prints a top-level branch labelled `wheat flour` holding those two dishes, sitting as a sibling of 'tossed in a sauce', 'finished at the table' and 'scattered over' — a coating word posing as an answer to the after question. Worse, in the default 'By coating' reading the empty cell truncates their fry chips through the single-leaf shortcut in grow(): Broasted renders as 'seasoned with paprika — Broasted chicken' with **'fried under pressure' dropped from the tree entirely**, and Southern loses 'in a skillet of lard'. Fix: give both an explicit chip — after: ["nothing after the fry"]. I ran it: the branch becomes 'nothing after the fry · wheat flour → {Southern fried chicken, Broasted chicken}' and both fry chips come back. This also makes the family's own argument, that the last column is a decision, include the decision to do nothing.

Chicken katsu's note says 'Flour then egg then crumb is the ladder every breaded cutlet on this table climbs' — and Milanesa de pollo, in the same table, does not climb it; its own note says 'there is no flour step at all'. Two fixes needed together. (a) Reword to something like 'the ladder every breaded cutlet here climbs but one'. (b) The shared chip is buried in third position, so the tree cannot fork on it — same defect the rice review blocked for 'crust wanted'. Reorder to Chicken katsu coat: ["breadcrumb","through flour and egg first","panko"] and Chicken schnitzel coat: ["breadcrumb","through flour and egg first","fine dry crumb"], Milanesa unchanged. Verified output: 'breadcrumb → through flour and egg first → {panko — Chicken katsu, fine dry crumb — Chicken schnitzel}' with Milanesa branching off at 'breadcrumb → fine dry crumb' — the note's point drawn by the tree instead of asserted beside it.

Two region cells contradict the table's own claims. Toriten is filed under 'Oita' while its note calls it 'Oita's version' and its marinade is karaage's chip for chip — yet 'By region' puts it in a different top-level branch from karaage and katsu. Nashville hot chicken is filed under 'Nashville' while carrying parent 'Southern fried chicken' — so the child sits outside its parent's region branch. Two-chip region cells are house-standard (noodle-soup.json uses ["Japan","Tokyo"], ["Vietnam","Saigon"]). Set Toriten region: ["Japan","Oita"] and Nashville region: ["American South","Nashville"]. Verified: 'Japan → {Karaage, Oita — Toriten, Chicken katsu}' and 'American South → {Southern fried chicken, Nashville — Nashville hot chicken}'. Strongly recommended in the same pass: Chicken 65 ["India","Tamil Nadu"] and Chicken pakora ["India","Punjab"], which yields an India branch instead of two more singletons.

'On frying twice' overclaims against its own table: 'That is why the twice-fried dishes are the ones that get sauced'. Karaage is twice-fried and is not sauced — it goes out with a lemon wedge, three rows above. The true statement is the converse. Rewrite along the lines of: 'That is why every dish here that meets a wet sauce after the fryer either goes in twice — yangnyeom and dakgangjeong are engineered to survive a glaze — or has no coating to lose, which is how Buffalo wings get away with a single fry. Karaage fries twice for itself, not for a sauce.'

Milanesa's note asserts 'both look back to Milan and neither descends from the other'. The half about Vienna is the Radetzky anecdote, which surfaced in the 1960s and which food historians do not credit; the half about Argentina is solid — the milanesa really does come from the cotoletta alla milanese with Italian immigration. Presenting them as symmetric states a debunked legend as shared origin. Suggested rewrite of the last sentence: 'Not a schnitzel variant — the milanesa came from the cotoletta alla milanese with Italian immigrants, while Vienna's Milanese origin is a story Vienna tells rather than a documented descent. Neither descends from the other.'
Spelling: 'Ayam goreng kalasan' → 'Ayam goreng Kalasan'. Kalasan is a district near Yogyakarta, so it takes a capital, the way the dish name is written everywhere including the linked source.

The two framing lines undercount the table they introduce. blocked.name: Frozen dessert
blocking: The standfirst and root exclude one of your own dishes. Root says 'A sweetened liquid · taken below freezing' and the standfirst opens 'All of these are a sweetened liquid taken below freezing' - but Halo-halo's base is 'plain water' with body 'nothing added', and its own note says the ice itself is bare. The sweetening happens after the freezing. Either give the root a clause that admits ice sweetened afterwards, or make 'sweetened after freezing' the chip that distinguishes halo-halo rather than leaving the row silently contradicting the premise.

Gelato's body cannot be 'egg yolk custard' alone. There is no single gelato tradition: northern crema-style gelato uses yolks, Sicilian gelato is thickened with cornstarch and is usually egg-free (adopted specifically to be lighter in Sicilian summers). Since the egg fork is one of the four things your standfirst promises, asserting gelato is always custard is wrong. Best fix: add a second row 'Gelato (Sicilian)' with body ['starch'] - it is a genuine fork, it gives the 'On giving water a body' note a fifth answer, and it balances the Italy entries. Minimum fix: change the body chips and say in the note that yolks are the northern convention.

French ice cream and Frozen custard are the same name in the law you cite on that very dish. 21 CFR 135.110(f)(1): at 1.4 percent egg yolk solids or more the product 'may be named frozen custard or french ice cream or french custard ice cream'. You present them as parent and child and hang that exact section on the child. Add a clause to the frozen custard note saying US law treats the two names as synonyms and that the split here is culinary - overrun and serving temperature - not legal. Also soften the sherbet note's claim that sherbet 'is the only dish here whose lineage is a legal definition', which the frozen custard note already contradicts.

The Bingsu row is modern milk-snow bingsu but is not labelled as such, and its note gives the shaved-ice move to the wrong tradition. Traditional patbingsu is shaved water ice with red bean, tteok and condensed milk; shaving a frozen milk block is a 2000s-2010s cafe development. And 'Halo-halo's move applied to dairy' makes halo-halo the origin of a technique it did not originate - halo-halo itself descends from Japanese kakigori, brought to Manila by Japanese migrants in the 1920s-30s via the mongo-ya stalls. Two fixes: name the row for what it is ('Bingsu (milk snow)' or mention uyu bingsu in the note), and reword the note so neither tradition is made the parent of the other. Strongly consider adding Kakigori as a row - right now the shaved-ice branch has two descendants and no ancestor, which is the same 'one tradition as the default' problem your dough-with-filling standfirst calls out by name.

Dondurma's note claims something I believe is false: 'slow enough to melt that it can be sold from an unrefrigerated cart'. Vendors keep it in a chilled churn and work it constantly with long-handled paddles precisely to keep it workable - the paddling is the mechanism, not evidence that the cold is unnecessary. Replace with the consequence that is actually true and more interesting: it can be served on a stick, sliced with a knife, and eaten with a fork.

The note 'On giving water a body' does not survive its own examples. It opens 'Frozen sugar-water has nothing holding it together', then names four answers, three of which are not water: egg yolk in France is a cream base, Maras is milk, kulfi is boiled-down milk. Only faloodeh is actually frozen sugar-water. Meanwhile the one dish that IS frozen sugar-water - sorbet - is absent, and its answer (sugar concentration doing structural work) sits in its own note instead. Either retitle to 'On what holds it together' and drop the water framing, or keep the water framing and use the dishes that are genuinely water-based: sorbet's sugar, faloodeh's starch noodles, granita accepting the crystals, halo-halo adding everything afterwards.
reasons: Checks 1-5 pass cleanly. All 16 rows are distinct. The two closest pairs are Sorbet / Helado de paila (separated only by the extra freeze chip 'turned by hand in a copper pan' plus region) and Halo-halo / Bingsu (separated only by base) - both are real distinctions and both survive.

No dead column. All five facets fork: base has 5 kinds, body 8, freeze 3 roots, air 5 values, region 11. Air in particular earns its place - it is the only thing separating Frozen custard from French ice cream, and Gelato from Philadelphia style.

No compound chips. Nothing is joined by a comma or 'and'; dondurma's salep and mastic are correctly split into two chips rather than one 'salep and mastic', which is right given lib/canon.ts builds a trie over individual chips.

Every multi-chip cell leads with the shared move. I checked all 13. This matters more than it looks: pathOf() in /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/src/lib/canon.ts concatenates chips in order across facets, so the first chip in a cell IS the fork - 'churned while freezing' first for frozen custard, soft serve, gelato, dondurma and paila; 'fruit puree' first for sherbet; 'milk base' first for kulfi, dondurma and frozen yogurt; 'egg yolk custard' first for semifreddo.

parent usage is mostly right. Sherbet -> Sorbet is exactly the 'X plus one thing' the CanonDish type comment asks for. Soft serve and Bingsu correctly have no parent despite sitting next to relatives. Frozen custard -> French ice cream is the weak one: it is minus two things (air taken out, hardening skipped) plus a region move, not plus one - and see the blocking note about what US law actually calls it.

Coverage is not parochial. Eleven regions across five continents; the US carries 5 of 16, but each of those five is a genuinely distinct fork rather than filler. The one real gap is structural, not geographic - see the kakigori point in blocking.

Facts I verified and that hold: Ibarra 1897 and ice carried from the glacier on Imbabura (the founder was Rosalia Suarez, worth naming in the note); faloodeh from Shiraz and among the oldest surviving frozen desserts; 4.5 pounds to the gallon in 21 CFR 135.110 (which also sets 1.6 lb total solids per gallon, if you want a second number); sherbet at 1-2 percent milkfat in 21 CFR 135.140; granita raked with a fork every half hour is the correct traditional and home method, though Messina and Palermo run smoother than Catania if you want a line on that.

blocked.name: Pancake
blocking: Two lift cells file a non-chemical aerator under 'chemical leavening', which is factually wrong. Okonomiyaki has lift: ["chemical leavening", "grated yam"] — grated nagaimo is a mechanical aerator and binder, not a chemical leavener. Æbleskiver has lift: ["chemical leavening", "whipped egg white"] — whipped whites are folded-in air, also not chemical. The second chip reads as an apposition naming the agent (it does exactly that for American stack: chemical leavening → baking powder), so both cells assert something untrue. The family contradicts itself on this: the Poffertjes note says 'yeast instead of egg white', treating egg white as æbleskiver's lift, and the Okonomiyaki note never mentions a chemical agent at all. Fix by making the lead chip true of what sits under it — e.g. Okonomiyaki lift: ["beaten air", "grated yam"] (or whatever category word the family settles on for mechanical lift), and Æbleskiver either lift: ["beaten air", "whipped egg white"] or, if the recipe genuinely uses both, ["chemical leavening", "baking powder", "whipped egg white"].

The standfirst is false for two of its own sixteen rows. 'Every one of these is ground starch slackened with liquid and set on direct heat': Latke has no ground starch and nothing slackened — its own note says 'The starch is the vegetable itself' and 'Nothing is poured' — and Dutch baby is baked (surface: 'hot oven'), not set on direct heat. The `root` line 'Ground starch · liquid · a hot surface' has the same ground-starch problem, though 'hot surface' survives via the preheated skillet. Rewrite the opening claim so it covers all sixteen (grated starch as well as ground; a hot pan, griddle or the skillet in an oven), or name the two outliers rather than letting the claim swallow them.

Bánh xèo is the only dish whose surface cell declares no turning decision. Every other row commits — 'flipped once', 'one side only', 'never turned', 'turned into a sphere' — but Bánh xèo reads ["shallow pan", "generous oil", "folded over"], and it is in fact cooked on one side under a lid and then folded, never flipped. Add the chip: ["shallow pan", "generous oil", "one side only", "folded over"], matching Apam balik's order. Then fix the 'On not turning it over' note, which currently claims baghrir and apam balik are the only two and is therefore wrong.

Chip order in two surface cells puts the specific move ahead of the shared one, so the trie forks the same decision at two different depths. Rendering 'By cooking surface' today: flat griddle → flipped once holds American stack, Crêpe, Okonomiyaki and Cachapa, while Jianbing, Jianbing guozi and Hotteok — all also flipped once — sit in separate 'spread with a scraper' and 'pressed flat' branches beside it, so the reader sees 'flipped once' twice at two levels and cannot tell it is one decision. Reorder to Jianbing and Jianbing guozi: ["flat griddle", "flipped once", "spread with a scraper"], Hotteok: ["flat griddle", "flipped once", "pressed flat"]. The turn is shared by seven dishes and the spreading move by two, so the turn must lead and the spread must fork beneath it.

Two notes assert things their chips do not carry. Bánh xèo's note rests on an ingredient that appears nowhere in its row — 'Coconut milk in the batter and enough oil to fry rather than griddle are what make it shatter' — while the batter cell reads only rice flour and turmeric; add "coconut milk" to that cell, since the note makes it the reason for the dish. And Dutch baby's note opens 'No leavening at all' while its own lift chip says 'steam alone' under a column labelled Leavening; make it 'No added leavening' so the row and the prose agree.

Two soft flags below, plus the harder errors in blocking.

Soft flag, not blocking: Crêpe is filed to Brittany with wheat flour, while Brittany's actual emblem — the buckwheat galette de sarrasin — is absent. Either 'France' is the safer region for the wheat crêpe, or the galette deserves its own row (it would fork cleanly: none / thin / buckwheat, and it is the savoury half of the same crêperie).

Soft flag, not blocking: Hotteok's surface reads 'flat griddle' with no oil chip, but the street version is cooked in a real slick of oil — nearer Pajeon's 'generous oil' than a dry griddle. Worth a second look.

Soft flag, not blocking: the register cell leads inconsistently for the three dishes that go both ways — Crêpe and Cachapa lead 'sweet', Blini leads 'savoury'. Because the trie nests chip under chip, Crêpe renders as 'sweet · savoury' and Blini lands in a different branch, so 'refuses to pick a side' never reads as a group. Deliberate defaults may justify it; flagging so it is a choice rather than an accident.

Not a defect in this family: 'By region' collapses to a near-flat list (14 of 16 branches hold one dish). Every other family in data/canon has the same shape, so it is house convention, not something to fix here.

Check 8 (standfirst) and check 4 (chip order) are where this fails — details in blocking. The prose is otherwise excellent: the notes explain mechanism rather than praise food, and 'On the dimpled pan' ('The pan is a constraint, not an answer') is the sharpest line in the set.
